I like the point he made about, how the mother goddess and polytheism was an intuitive move or "religion" , while monotheism is counterintuitive. Which is true if what you care about is the outside, the life problems and needs that you have, for example, you have a problem with artistic creativity you pray to the god of music , you're having a war , pray to the god of war ....etc . But as humanity evolved, few people begun to care for not the outside, but for their inside, they looked inside of themselves because the outside wasn't any kinder  even with all the gods around. And monotheism started at the center of the world (more or less) an area where civilizations connect , the Egyptian civilization, the Persian, the mesopotamian. An area so powerful, so advanced yet so cruel , to their own people and others, and the people in between those lands witnessing all those cultures, and being subjected to thei cruelty sometimes, not having much to hold on to , not having their life crowded by much possessions, or even much beauty besides the night sky, being mostly surrounded by miles of desserts, the outside world becomes very little of importance, and you must find what "truly" matters in life besides the outside, so you'd look inside of you, you'd stay up at night admiring the majestic, free , endless beauty of the night sky , getting as much of it as you can, just you and the sky , reflecting on it and yourself and anything that has encountered you during your life , any questions you ever had about all of it , and as you go for months or years like that , your life becomes lighter, your mind is lighter..... And at one night it would click , that  to have a good life, you don't need the goddess of fertility, or the god of war on your side .... You just need to admire ( love) and be curious, look at the world with curiosity and admiration, because what is the point of it all , you don't own anything in this world at all , it was belonging to someone else before you or and it will belong to someone else after you .............. except, what you know and what you have felt. And it clicks again, if you only own what you know and what you have felt, could this all be a test ? To know who's good and who's not ? But again you think about how the civilizations around you are behaving and they're supposedly the "godly " people, and how materialistic their rituals are , sometimes even cruel and diabolical. But now you know that the most important things in life are non materialistic, which are admiration (love) and curiosity, so how can these things be non materialistic and endless and beautiful, but the gods are of material( the mesopotamian gods as examples, the moon , the sun and the morning star ) , demand materialistic things for themselves to give rewards , and can be so cruel in their demands ,( still looking at the night sky btw) AND THEN THE BIG QUESTION, while you're looking at the sky , you notice how the gods are numbered (finite) 3 to some, 26 to some, 78 to others , while the stars are so much and so many , each of them could be a god , so why did people stop the count of god's at 3 or 78 or even more but never as big of a number as the stars you could count in one sit , so it's either the number of gods is way more than what each say if not infinite, or ....... You look at the big picture...... The "non material" thing that's connecting all those stars , the moon , the sun ...... It's the sky around them , it's one sky , so big , it fits all of them and all the world inside it . And it clicks once agai, it's not gods it god , people have been so distracted by first what's on the land ( fire , trees, rivers , animals , the sea) and seeing how powerful and prosperous they are , then they looked up and saw the moon the sun , the stars and planets even and saw how majestic and powerful they are, but the true power was always their at plain sight holding everything together, the sky . The sky is not a material, it's one and only,  one everywhere and every time, wherever you go in the world there's sky all the time. Then if that's god , then it is the god of everything inside the sky , moon , sun , fertility, war , love , music....... , and since it is non material it wouldn't want anything material to give rewards, maybe it would reward good people, the people who ask questions? The people who admire the world?..... Or the people that walked the extra mile to know that god , know the truth, who saw behind the stars , saw the sky for it's power , how it easily contains everything within it so gracefully, almost so lovingly.... Maybe that is what the sky ( god) always wanted, for us to admire the world, be curious about it , and be loving and graceful like the sky , then only we can fit so many burning flames (stars/problems) and the heaviness of the world without FALLING or breaking. So monotheism now doesn't seem so counter intuitive , in fact all that has preceded it start seeming limited, and monotheism begins to be very intuitive, almost like it has existed all along, it just needed someone to walk the extra mile to bump into it , to look beyond the stars .  ( This is just my theory on how it might have started, then of course it will develop into what we know today about all the extra lore , this is just the seed that started the thought of one and only god , later developing into a full tree🌲 with roots and branches). Professor Jiang's lecture is a highly effective and accurate primer on the Gnostic worldview. He correctly explains its core beliefs, its interpretation of scripture, and its fundamental opposition to both mainstream Christianity and modern materialism.
However, the framing of the lecture as revealing the "Secret History" and the "Birth of Evil" is a rhetorical choice. He presents the Gnostic belief system as the factual, hidden truth. A mainstream historian or theologian would present it as a fascinating and influential religious-philosophical movement from late antiquity that was ultimately suppressed by Orthodox Christianity but whose ideas have resonated in Western esoteric traditions for centuries.

Interesting lecture. A few thoughts on what you've presented here and previously.

- In a previous lecture you mentioned how Monotheism, essentially, is not something intuitively arrived at and came about by way of accident, and in this lecture, noted how it is adopted as a tool of Empire after a period of societal evolution; relegating it to something arbitrary, utilitarian (a tool of control and propaganda) and stripped of divine providence. Whilst a radical/provocative claim (and somewhat subversive, but I'm curious to see the end point of this series, so have opted to reserve judgement till then), note that such a stance runs contrary to your adoption of Geist in the previous lecture. 

Geist was presented therein as a mystical, near Gnostic force of collective consciousness, or a spiritual 'cloud', that connects human minds to the Monad. This is a rather cursory explanation of Hegel that leaves out a crucial point: the collective consciousness includes and partakes in all conscious ideas. In other words, in this system, there are no accidents.  

To better understand Geist (and in turn Hegel), it can be thought of as the dynamic, rational process through which the Absolute (ultimate reality: truth, freedom and God) comes to know itself through history. For Hegel, history is a dialectical progression of ideas (thesis) meeting opposition (antithesis), resolving into a higher synthesis, advancing Geist’s self-understanding through human culture, institutions and ideas. The end point is absolute self-consciousness (Geist or Spirit coming to know itself as Spirit). Monotheism, especially Christianity (Hegel is a Christian philosopher after all), is not accidental but a crucial stage in Geist’s self-realisation. In other words, Christianity is historically necessary.

Christianity for Hegel then is a revealed religion that uniquely expresses the Absolute in conceptual form, and Christian tenets are central to his philosophy. The Incarnation for instance demonstrates the idea that God becomes human in Christ (a God-man unity), reflecting Geist’s reconciliation of the infinite (divine) and finite (human). More than a theological claim this is a philosophical truth by way of the Absolute manifesting in history, uniting spirit and matter. As for the Trinity, Hegel sees it as a clear dialectical structure: the Father is the universal divine idea (thesis), the Son is its particular manifestation in the world (antithesis), and the Holy Spirit is their synthesis in human community and consciousness, driving history forward. Further,  Christianity’s emphasis on salvation through faith reflects Geist’s movement toward freedom as humans recognise their divine nature and overcome alienation from the Absolute. This culminates in the modern state (per Hegel), where freedom is realised through rational institutions.

So far from being accidental, monotheism (Judaism, then Christianity) is essential for Hegel. It shifts from polytheism’s fragmented gods to a single, universal God, aligning with Geist’s rational unity. Christianity refines this necessarily by making God immanent (present in history via Christ), thereby enabling humans to grasp the Absolute conceptually. 

Ultimately, these are quite complicated concepts that require nuance, and care should be taken not to conflate them given surface level similarities with other ideas and philosophical systems. 

- Regarding Milton, while quite a few prominent historical figures have arguably been part of Secret Societies or flirted with Gnostic ideals, Milton doesn't seem to be one of them. He possessed some heretical beliefs but these were Arian in nature (that Jesus was created by God; not one with God), not Gnostic. Milton himself was a staunch Protestant. 

- You're reading intent into Milton's work that arguably doesn't exist. The whole point of Paradise Lost is an exploration of theodicy: the attempted justification of the justice of God, focusing on free will, evil (Satan, sin, the Fall) and redemption with regards to God’s omnibenevolent and omnipotent nature. Satan is a purposefully complex character, arguably charismatic and rhetorically compelling (as seen in the quoted passages), but Milton does not intend him to be sympathetic or correct. He is deceitful and prideful, and a sympathetic reading of Satan falls into the very trap Christianity and Milton warn against: that evil is tempting/seductive, easily deceptive and intentionally subversive. Ultimately, Paradise Lost reinforces that God is just, Satan is the adversary, and humanity’s salvation comes through repentance and God’s grace.

- Paradise Lost cannot be read independent to Paradise Regained, which explores Christ’s temptation in the wilderness. Christ’s rejection of Satan’s offers therein demonstrates perfect obedience to God in contrast to Adam and Eve. Christ then is presented as a kind of 'second Adam' whose victory restores the paradise lost through the Fall, fulfilling God's redemptive plan. Satan herein is depicted as pathetically impotent; he is humiliated by his failure, and his rebellion (neither heroic or truthful) is foiled. These ideas are perfectly aligned with mainstream Christian thought. 

- Again, reserving judgement until the series ends, but there's a slight contradiction/cognitive dissonance in how these ideas are being presented. On the one hand you are setting the stage for Gnosticism as a kind of secret knowledge, an ultimate truth, thereby endorsing it contrary to Christianity, which is presented as a tool of control, propaganda and Empire (a point I contest and disagree with, but can engage with intellectually). To be clear, I'm not sure if this is your intent, but that's how it's currently coming across. On the other hand, being a secret knowledge, Gnosticism is being held as foundational to power structures that benefit The Powers That Be (TPTB), and a knowledge possessed by the elites. If that is the case, its truth value is diminished in light of its moral shortcomings (such as the idea of 'sin for salvation', which you touched upon). It seems you are suggesting either:

1) Charitably: This is the secret truth of existence (hence why you claim it makes more sense than Christianity), which the elites posses, and knowing this truth allows you to better understand TPTB and resist manipulation by the elites, or
2) You are subverting Christianity, a Western foundational structure, by presenting it as a tool of empire and propaganda while elevating Gnosticism as a truer alternative that is, in and of itself, a perversion of Christianity. 

But therein is the tension. Gnosticism cannot be both true and good; you cannot endorse it as the enlightened take contra Christianity whilst simultaneously setting it up as a critique of the elites' worldview, particularly when it justifies evil, presents evil as good, and whose adherents think themselves superior to the masses and would be as Gods themselves. You mentioned Christianity as presented to you in the West (Canada) didn't make much sense, but confusion should not be an excuse for distortion. As you've built quite the following, some care needs to be taken in presenting these ideas, as nuance can easily be lost in favour of academic provocation.

I'll finish with this: Christianity’s vision and purpose is best encapsulated, in my view, by this Orthodox maxim: “God became man so that man may become God”. It's this divine love that surpasses Gnosticism’s elitist and morally ambiguous temptations, wherein all can unite with God through Christ. And if Christianity is true, then anything contrary (including Gnosticism) is a tool of evil/Satan to subvert and corrupt souls away from God/Christ.

Nevertheless, I look forward to seeing how your series unfolds.

For one, very common is the mother and son theme. Specifically a son who corresponds with the sun (a sun god). Where the son is sacrificed and is resurrected. There's Sophia, Ishtar, Cybele, Mary etc. Zeus's mother poisoned cronos to save him. 

I'm not sure whether these themes began pure and were corrupted, or began corrupted and was watered down for the public to accept. Maybe they're still pure and beyond the construct of good vs evil. 

There's also patterns with hermaphrodite and castration of the son. Some religions practiced this by castrating the priests, also knights templar seemed to have practiced it along with other current secret societies (sometimes with unwilling participants). Principles of alchemy is often at the root of these things, turning lead into gold. Rituals being part of this process of turning something base into a valuable commodity like paper money into gold and silver, imagination into manifestation, bodily fluids into potions etc.

Great breakdown. For those looking for historical context, these *Gnostic* ideas (Sethian/Valentinian) manifested in several major movements:

→ *Manichaeism:* The foundation of medieval dualism.

→ *Bogomilism:* The bridge between the East and the West.

→ *The Bosnian Church:* The most mysterious of the "heretical" churches.

The Bosnian Church is particularly interesting because it shows these "secret" beliefs functioning as an official national faith, resisting external crusades for centuries.

### **@monkcoder7580**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgGfQdv_rPc&lc=Ugx_NQaQwVegYSjd87F4AaABAg)

Love this lecture — it’s a powerful narrative. But for balance, it’s worth noting that mainstream archaeology doesn’t see the “mother-goddess → matriarchy → male rebellion → patriarchy → monotheism” sequence as a proven, linear history.

Yes, female figurines are ancient and widespread. Yes, agriculture changed inheritance and social structures. But many archaeologists argue that figurines don’t automatically prove matriarchal political systems, and marriage-like institutions existed even among hunter-gatherers. The transition to patriarchy appears to be complex, regionally varied, and multi-causal — not a single global shift.

It’s a fascinating hypothesis, but it remains debated rather than settled historical fact.

### **@Gabs_Faria** | 👍 1 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgGfQdv_rPc&lc=UgwJJE7zqxZnzY77Gv94AaABAg)

Great lecture by Prof. Jiang explaining the history of what these secret societies and esoteric groups actually believe. However, as a Christian watching this, I think it's really important to point out that the whole "God is a monster created by Sophia" idea isn't some deep, hidden truth—it's just classic 2nd-century Gnosticism, which the early church already dealt with thoroughly.
Here are a few historical and theological pushbacks on the secret society worldview presented here:

The "Monster" God (Sophia & The Demiurge): The Gnostics fundamentally hated the physical world and tried to merge Greek Platonism with Christianity hundreds of years after Jesus. If the creator God was an ignorant mistake made by Sophia, he isn't God by definition. The biblical God isn't a confused, lesser demiurge; He is the uncaused First Cause who created the material world and called it "very good." The ultimate proof that the physical world isn't evil is the Incarnation—God Himself taking on a human body.
 
The Bible as "Propaganda" (1:06:26): The claim that the Bible is just political propaganda to consolidate power completely ignores early Christian history. If it was a propaganda tool for earthly power, why was it written, preserved, and spread by poor, marginalized people? The early Christians and apostles were brutally tortured and martyred by the Roman Empire for refusing to worship the emperor. You don't willingly die an excruciating death for a political lie you just invented. Furthermore, the Bible is a library of dozens of books written over 1,500 years by over 40 authors across three continents, yet it maintains a beautifully unified theological message. That’s not a top-down propaganda campaign.
 
The "Inner Light" and Relativism (1:08:18): The idea the professor mentions at the end—that "it's okay to do evil, just listen to the light inside you"—is literally the oldest lie in the book. It’s the exact temptation from the Garden of Eden in Genesis 3 ("You will be like God"). Relying purely on our own "inner light" is just dangerous moral relativism. If I am my own ultimate moral compass, what stops me from doing terrible things and justifying it as "finding my truth"? We are flawed, and we need an objective standard of goodness and a Savior, not a romanticized view of our own sins.
If anyone wants to see how the early Christians completely dismantled this exact "Sophia/Demiurge" myth, check out the book "Against Heresies" by Irenaeus of Lyons, written way back in the 2nd century. It's fascinating how these "secret" society ideas are really just recycled ancient heresies!
